answers.text: Tell the assistant: always give exactly three lines, in this fixed order — delivery date, then item and quantity, then any change from the original order — each line just that one fact and nothing else, so it's clear where one line ends. If any of the three isn't mentioned in the email, write 'not stated' rather than skip the line. That way it always comes out the same.

Structure: date, amount, category, submitter for each claim, then a total line at the bottom that's just the sum of the amounts column. If two lines look like duplicates — same date and amount — flag them separately rather than merging them so nothing gets lost in the total.
There's an error in the dates — the call was on the 14th and the new delivery date is the 19th, that's five days later, not three days out like the email says.
The 15% delivery increase checks out, 54 to 62 is about right. But the on-time rate doesn't — 3 late out of 62 is closer to 95%, not 97% like it says.

I'd sign off the second one, it shows the actual sales and returns figures so you can see how the 4.1% was worked out. The first one just gives the percentage with no way to see if it's right without redoing the whole calculation yourself.

I'd send the second one as is, it's got the order reference and the credit reference so it's easy to check later. The first one could still be fine, but there's no order number in it so right now you can't confirm it's even the right order before it goes out.
1. No, that's the customer's own info. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. Yes, it's out already. 5. No.

The pricing and volume discount numbers I'd hold back, and the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies. The delivery schedule is fine to paste as is, nothing sensitive in dates and quantities.

Before the report goes to my supervisor each week, I'd cross-check the delivery total and the on-time rate against the raw log in the system, not just trust the AI's summary numbers. That way if a number's been made up or miscalculated it gets caught before it's sent up.

The step that worries me most is the last one, where the confirmation goes out automatically if stock shows available — once that email's sent you can't take it back. I'd also watch the first step, since if the AI misreads the quantities everything downstream is wrong. The gate on step four should check that the extracted quantities match what's actually recorded in the warehouse system before anything gets sent.
